title: Paramitas - Perfection of Conduct (Sīla)
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona's talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating gratitude and letting go of attachment to things we already possess. This is rooted in the concept of sila, or perfection of conduct, which is a key aspect of the Buddhist path. By practicing right speech, action, and livelihood according to the eightfold path, we can recognize and release our attachment to material possessions and cultivate a more mindful and compassionate way of living.

sentences.text: Good evening, fearless bodhisattvas.
That's you.
Continuing the lessons from children that Kate started, with the boy who was bouncing the ball and was so intently happy just bouncing it, I've got a story recently from my family.
My niece and nephew started third and fourth grade recently, so their grandmother gave them back-to-school gifts.
My niece got some bright pink cowboy boots with silver laces, and my nephew got a cowboy shirt with gold trim.
They opened up their gifts and they were all excited.
Then my nephew looks over and says, "Why didn't I get cowboy boots?"
His father said, "Do you want cowboy boots?"
And he said, "No."
Does that sound familiar?
"Oh, I want that."
"Do you really want that?"
"Oh, no, I guess not."
That ties for me into the talk Tim gave last week about gratitude, because I have the experience sometimes of seeing something and desire arises.
Desire.
"Oh, I've already got that."
And that's great as far as we can take it.
When the experience does arise where we have desire for something we already have, there's an opportunity for gratitude.
That's not to say there aren't plenty of times when it's "Oh, look at that house, I wish I had a house like that," just after you've been kicked out of your apartment.
But recognizing opportunities for gratitude when they're there makes it easier to recognize opportunities for gratitude that aren't so bright.
Other talks we've been doing lately have been on the paramitas, the perfections.
We talked about the perfection of giving, Dhanaparamita.
I guess that's probably a couple of months back now.
And then Edie talked about the perfection of effort.
So let's look tonight at sila, which is the perfection of conduct.
Reviewing our basic Buddhist philosophy, going back to Buddhism 101: Shakyamuni Buddha taught the four noble truths.
The general character of this life is dissatisfaction.
That's the first noble truth.
Number two, the origin of that dissatisfaction is clinging, our attachment to things that aren't real.
Noble truth number three, relief is possible.
And noble truth number four is the eightfold path.
What is the eightfold path?
The first two are right view and right intention, which are grouped in the wisdom category.
Then there's right speech, right action, and right livelihood, which are grouped in the conduct category.
And finally, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are grouped in the concentration category.
So that middle category, the conduct category, from the eightfold path shows up again in the paramitas, the perfections.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood started out, in the original monastic teaching of the Buddha, as the Vinyana Code: some 250 precepts that the monks were expected to live by.
I spent a couple of years living on a sailboat where I had 90 square feet of living space, and I thought that was a little cramped.
But one of those 250 says the monks are not allowed to live in a hut any larger than 56 square feet.
There are other such original precepts, such as the monks shall not walk more than 30 miles carrying raw wool, or shall not teach the Dharma to somebody carrying an umbrella.
Those very specific precepts, in the evolution into Mahayana, boiled down into something more general: how do we conduct our lives so as not to cause harm?

Dogen, it is believed the founder of the Soto Zen school in Japan, ordained under 58 precepts, and what he passed on to his priests, they ordained under, were the 16 that we practice regularly in the school today.
So it's been just about a thousand years we've been stuck with these 16.
What is the difference between beneficial conduct and perfection of conduct?
Similar to what we talked about with Dhanaparamita, the perfection of giving happens as we gradually realize there's not a distinction between the giver, the receiver, and the gift.

Conduct for the benefit of all beings gradually happens with the recognition that the other beings are not distinct from this collection that I call a being, from the interdependence of the existence of all beings.
When I say this collection that I call a being, this self, Robert Aitken pointed specifically: I am only my settings, interacting with all my past settings, nothing more.
So from that perspective of causation, of karma, there are memories and thoughts and those sorts of phenomena that arise and mix with each other through causation and cause current ones.
That's our story, the story we're living now.
And we have the opportunity to react to that story, oftentimes with dissatisfaction.
In Dogen's Genjokoan, we chant:
*When actualized by the myriad things, your body and mind as well as the bodies and minds of others drop away.
No trace of realization remains, and this no trace continues endlessly.*
This story continues endlessly, and yet attachment drops away.
Then there's the Diamond Sutra, the fundamental dialogue from the Diamond Sutra.
Subhuti asks Tatagatabuddha, exact quote here:
*If someone sets forth on the Bodhisattva path, how should they stand?
How should they walk?
And how should they control their thoughts?*
Which is conduct, right?
How do you stand?
How do you walk?
How do you control your thoughts?
He's in essence asking about conduct.
And when he's asking about the Bodhisattva path, he's asking specifically about that perfection of conduct.
He's asking about sila paramita.
The Buddha's response starts out, *someone who sets forth on the Bodhisattva path should give birth to this thought.*
That's the essence of the Buddha's response.
He's asked about walking and standing and our day-to-day conduct, and the Buddha's bringing it back and saying it starts out with this thought.
And how else are we going to manage giving birth to a thought, or paying attention to thought, but through meditation?
I'm going to digress a moment from the Diamond Sutra.

I don't think we've talked recently about the sexism that existed in the early Buddhist teaching, and that the Buddha only grudgingly and belatedly acknowledged that women are just as capable of becoming enlightened as men.
Oh, and even so, women have to be subservient.
The nuns have to be subservient to the monks, and there are these extra hundred rules they have to follow.
So, in the context of those extra hundred rules, a story.
Because of some happenstance of those rules, there were no nuns in Thailand until the 20th century.
Venerable Bhikkhuni Boromai Kabir Singh was the first Thai woman to receive full ordination as a Bhikkhuni, as a nun.
As required in Bhikkhuni ordinations, she took 311 precepts.
A young man who was visiting her asked, "How can you keep all 311 precepts?"
She answered, "I only keep one precept."
The young man, surprised, asked, "What is that?"
She replied, "I just watch my mind."
So maybe she knew the core of the Diamond Sutra very well, and she probably did.
Probably also she just had a good life understanding that all those precepts come from that fundamental teaching of what the heck is going on right here, right now.
Anything out there is just part of the story that's feeding what's going on right here, right now.
So back to the Diamond Sutra.

Subhuti asks, *If someone sets forth on the Bodhisattva path, how should they stand, how should they walk, and how should they control their thoughts?* And Buddha responds to Subhuti, *Someone who sets forth on the Bodhisattva path should give birth to this thought:*
*In the realm of complete nirvana, I shall liberate all beings.
And while I thus liberate beings, not a single being is liberated.*
So there we have it.

That answer has two fundamental halves of one contradiction that the Bodhisattva path is about embracing: engaging with beings, going to liberate them all, and yet not becoming entangled in the story.
Engaging the story, but not being entangled with it, which might be simplified as just recognizing when we are entangled with it.
The focus is on the activity of this moment, not on the goal, not on some future state.
Do your best right now, and then let it go.
Which is certainly not easy, and something I have been working with lately is trying to recognize how that notion, which sounds simple from the start, doesn't happen.
First, there's the challenge of remembering to be compassionate, remembering the precepts, remembering concern for other beings.
Then, once that's remembered, there's the challenge of what path is really beneficial.
What do I do now?
And then, even if I was lucky enough to come up with the right answer to that, actually doing it is a whole other thing, right?
That brings us to our own precepts in Red Cedar Zen community.
They're the 16 that we chant in the full moon ceremony, the 16 that are part of the Jukai ceremony, where we publicly ask for help from the rest of the sangha.

After studying for a number of years, we ask the teacher for permission to sew the blue bib, which is really asking for permission to study the 16 precepts and to get help from everybody in the sangha in that study.
They're the same precepts that are part of our wedding ceremony, that are part of the priest ordination, and that are part of the transmission ceremony.
So that is a huge undertaking.
We're just going to mention them and leave it to other opportunities to study them individually.
*I take refuge in Buddha.
I take refuge in Dharma.
I take refuge in sangha, the community.
I vow to avoid harmful conduct.
I vow to do beneficial conduct.
I vow to live for and with all beings.
I vow to protect life, not to kill.
I vow to receive gifts, not to steal.
I vow to respect others, not to misuse sexuality.
I vow to be truthful, to not lie.
I vow to maintain clarity, not to intoxicate self or others.
I vow to speak kindly, not to speak ill of others.
I vow to maintain modesty, not to praise self at the expense of others.
I vow to be generous, not to be possessive of anything.
I vow to be loving, not to harbor ill will.
And I vow to cherish and polish the three treasures.*
So I was trying to picture breathing with each of those, breathing with each moment in each story, just paying attention to each breath.
It's like picking up yak poop, which is something that Diane and I have to do.
Sitting in meditation, we feel like it's another breath, another breath.
It's boring.
It's all the same.
But looking closely, the scoop of poop right in front of us, at times when we're able to look closely, really is fresh.
Sometimes it's light, fluffy and dried out.
Sometimes it's a sticky liquid.
Sometimes it's frozen and stuck to the ground.
Sometimes there are interesting things growing in it, mushrooms or flies, or maybe not.
So, back to sila.
We're slowly working toward less chasing and less beating ourselves up, and setting our sights on what can be done now to end suffering.
I'm going to reach for another story here on the precepts.
The slave Punika was a follower of the Buddha and attained the first stage of awakening while carrying water from the river to her master's house.
Sometime later, she was again bringing water from the river when she saw the Brahman Udkasudika taking a ritual bath.
She said to him, "I must come down to the river, even on cold days like today, because I am a water carrier and a slave.
But why do you come to the river, even when it makes you shiver with cold?
What are you afraid of?"
And here we can stick ourselves in that place, right?
Why do we do whatever we do that's seemingly ritual?
What are you afraid of?
What are you afraid of?
He said, "You know the laws of karma.
I am washing away my past evil acts."
"Who told you that would work?" she asked.
"If this were true, frogs, turtles, and water snakes would all go to heaven.
And evildoers like pork butchers, thieves, and executioners could all be cleansed with a bath.
Besides, doesn't water wash away your merit, too?
It would be better to avoid doing evil in the first place.
So spare yourself from the freezing water and go home."
The Brahmin saw the truth of her words and tried to give her his robe in gratitude.
But she refused.
Instead, she suggested that he should take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha and train in the precepts.
He took refuge and he said to her, "Your words have washed me clean."
What are we afraid of?
What are we doing that's really not beneficial?
We can at least work on the precepts, for whatever success we have with them, little by little.
We are the impact of our past settings on our present settings.
Fearless enlightened bodhisattvas do not hide from cause and effect.
Other times we hide from cause and effect because we're afraid.
Sometimes we can look at cause and effect squarely for what they are.
In fact, the work of the bodhisattva, that of liberating beings from suffering, depends on cause and effect.
What good would beneficial conduct do in the world if it were not for causation?
So next week we'll have the opportunity, all of us, to once again take those vows in the full moon ceremony and work on it a bit more.
We'll join you then.
May our intentions...
